Canons Regular
KAN-unz REG-yoo-lur
n. pl. (clergy living in community under the Rule of Augustine, bound to the choir office yet serving churches)
From Greek kanon, a measuring rod, a rule; with Latin regularis, living under a rule.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Canons regular are ordained clergy who live in community under a rule, chiefly the Rule of Augustine, and who keep the choir office as monks do while also serving churches, schools and hospitals. They emerged in the eleventh century out of reforming efforts to make cathedral and collegiate clergy live in common and hold no private property, and the Premonstratensians are their most famous order. The distinction from monks is substantial: a monk is a layman by origin whose business is his own sanctification within an enclosure, whereas a canon is a cleric whose business is public ministry. This dictionary records the canons because their hybrid is the nearest medieval approach to the New Testament's arrangement and because the gap that remains is the point. Scripture knows ordained men gathered in colleges of elders, “ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23), devoted to the word and to prayer rather than to administration, “give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Act 6:4). It also knows these men as householders, “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife” (1Ti 3:2). The canons took the college and the office and the ministry, and kept the one vow Scripture never imposes, so the household went missing, “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled” (Heb 13:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a canon as a church dignitary holding a prebend; regular as governed by rule; a college as a collection of persons with common duties; a cleric as one in holy orders; and community as common possession or society.

expand to see more

CANON, n. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend or revenue allotted for the performance of divine service in a cathedral or collegiate church.

REGULAR, adj. Governed by rule or rules; instituted or initiated according to established forms or discipline.

COLLEGE, n. In a general sense, a collection or assemblage; a society of men invested with certain powers, performing certain duties, or engaged in some common employment.

CLERICAL, adj. Relating to the clergy; as clerical errors; pertaining to a clerk or writer.

COMMUNITY, n. Common possession; as a community of goods; also, society at large, or a body of people having common rights.

Key Scripture

Act 14:23 — "And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed."

Act 6:4 — "But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word."

1Ti 3:2 — "A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;"

Heb 13:4 — "Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge."

Modern Corruption

Clergy in community under rule: the medieval arrangement closest to a college of elders, less the households Scripture assumes.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the college itself. Scripture does not leave a minister alone with a congregation; it appoints a body of men together, “ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23), and it guards their time for the work that only they can do, “give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Act 6:4). The canons built a structure that assumed clergy need one another, which is more than many modern churches assume.

The remaining error is the vow. Paul assumes an overseer has a wife and children and judges him partly by how he governs them, “the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour” (1Ti 3:2); a rule that forbids him the household removes the very evidence the apostle asks for. Where Scripture calls a thing honourable, “Marriage is honourable in all” (Heb 13:4), a rule that forbids it is a departure rather than a discipline, “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats” (1Ti 4:3).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kanon (G2583), a rule; Greek cheirotoneo (G5500), to appoint by vote; Greek proskartereo (G4342), to continue in; Greek episkopos (G1985), an overseer; Greek koluo (G2967), to forbid.

expand to see more

Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint, to ordain by stretched hands; “ordained them elders in every church”, Acts 14:23.

Greek diakonia (G1248) — service, ministry of the word; “the ministry of the word”, Acts 6:4.

Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer, a bishop; “A bishop then must be blameless”, 1 Timothy 3:2.

Greek timios (G5093) — honoured, held precious; “Marriage is honourable in all”, Hebrews 13:4.

Greek koluo (G2967) — to hinder, to forbid; “Forbidding to marry”, 1 Timothy 4:3.

Usage

"“ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) — the college the canons imitated well."

"“the husband of one wife” (1Ti 3:2) — the evidence their vow removed."

"“give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Act 6:4) — the work a rule should protect."
